# Independent audit: sampled peak, variation correction, and one-fine-coordinate budget



## 1. Sampled peak and exact adjacent interpolation

The sampled bases with nonempty fibers form a consecutive finite segment of the given arithmetic progression. This remains true when the extreme sampled fibers have zero s-volume. Brunn--Minkowski applied to every adjacent pair gives the stated root interpolation lower bound. The sampled roots are a nonnegative concave sequence, so their powers w_j are unimodal, including any maximum plateau.

For a unimodal sequence, choosing any peak index shows that adjacent minima sum to every term except that one peak: the sum is exactly T-W. Integrating over the disjoint adjacent grid intervals proves A>=h(T-W), with no grid-hull hypothesis and no reference to an unsampled maximum. Unsampled end pieces contribute only additional nonnegative volume.

The exact interpolation integral is

    Phi_s(a,b)=(sum_(j=0)^s a^j b^(s-j))/(s+1).

For a>=b>=0, each of the s-1 mixed terms is at least b^s, which gives the variation improvement

    Phi_s(a,b)>=b^s+(a^s-b^s)/(s+1).

Summing yields A>=h[T-W+TV(w)/(s+1)]. At s=1 there are no mixed terms and the statement is the trapezoid bound. At a=b or b=0 the algebra includes the endpoint cases exactly. The cone from a positive s-body on one grid level to a point on the next attains equality with TV=W, so 1/(s+1) cannot be increased in this universal correction.

For N>=1, unimodality gives TV=2W-w_0-w_(N-1), including N=1 where the same endpoint appears twice and TV=0. The resulting endpoint formula must not be read at N=0; the original empty-sum inequalities are still valid there.

## 2. Complete equality classification for the main inequality

If T>0 and N>=2, any unequal adjacent sampled weights force the root interpolation strictly above their minimum on a positive-length interval. Thus equality requires every sampled weight to equal the same W>0. Root concavity and continuity on the interior projection, together with integral equality, force actual section volume W everywhere between the extreme sampled bases.

Any nonempty fiber beyond those extreme bases would form a positive-volume cone with a full-volume extreme sampled fiber, adding positive volume outside the sampled range. Hence equality forces the projection endpoints to be exactly those sampled bases.

The two extreme fibers are full s-dimensional bodies with equal volume. Their midpoint Minkowski average lies in the actual midpoint fiber, whose volume is also W. The Brunn--Minkowski equality case therefore makes the extreme fibers translates. Every intermediate Minkowski interpolation is the corresponding translated copy, contained in an actual section of the same volume. Strict volume monotonicity for full-dimensional compact convex bodies gives equality of the sets. This proves precisely the affine-shear product representation, including s=1.

Conversely that representation has area h(N-1)W=h(T-W). For N=1 and T>0, equality A=0 holds exactly for a single vertical sampled s-body; any other base point creates a positive-volume cone. If T=0, equality is simply A=0. No positive-dimension assertion is hidden in the latter case.

## 3. Coarse-level summation and sharp depth budget

Summing the sampled-peak bound gives sum W_z>=T-M/h. Extra coarse levels without fine samples can be included in M: they only weaken this bound. J counts all levels with a nonempty sample, even if an individual level has zero sampled volume, and division by J is therefore valid. The positive part in the global peak estimate is retained.

The maximizing actual fine fiber has positive s-volume because T>0. Its ordinary continuous centroid is a point of the original source. Every containing ambient closed halfspace restricts to a containing s-dimensional halfspace or the whole fiber, so ordinary Grünbaum gives unnormalized mass at least Gamma_s times that fiber volume. The common fine covolume h cancels from normalized depth. This proves the stated correction

    max depth >=(Gamma_s/J)(1-M/(hT))_+.

The conditions J<=2^k and M/(hT)<=1/2 yield the exact target Gamma_s/2^(k+1). The proof does not infer either condition for a general source. In particular it does not replace J by a parity bound without proof.

The binary coarse cube times [0,h] times a fixed s-simplex has exactly 2^(k+1) equal fine fibers at exposed base vertices. Its ratio M/(hT) is 1/2. Every within-fiber cap can be extended to an ambient cap isolating that base. The exact ordinary simplex maximum Gamma_s then gives both the lower and upper depth bounds Gamma_s/2^(k+1). Thus the endpoint budget and the displayed bound are sharp in the stated family.

## 4. All cap directions and open-complement accounting

The sampled-peak inequality applies separately to every compact cut Q_z intersect H with its own sampled support and peak. These supports and maximizing fibers need not agree for different caps or between a cap and its complement; the proof never assumes they do.

For the open complement of H={ell>=0}, the compact convex sets Q_z intersect {ell<=-epsilon} increase to Q_z intersect {ell<0}. Coarse volumes and all sampled s-volumes converge monotonically. The original sampled base set is finite, so the maxima of those finitely many increasing section-volume sequences converge to the open-complement maximum. This proves the open inequality rigorously.

A closed cap and its open complement partition both measures exactly, including whole sampled fibers on a boundary plane. Adding their inequalities gives (14) without double counting. When the continuous x-normal is nonzero, every sampled boundary slice has zero s-volume, so replacing the open complement by the opposite closed halfspace preserves the relevant sampled maxima. Otherwise the open convention remains necessary, especially for pure-base cuts.

No missing volume factor, boundary contribution, or unsupported common-peak allocation was found.
